beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Bias in AI explains why fairness problems cannot be reduced to biased training data.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its course follows harmful pathways through measurement, language models, retrieval, and agent decisions.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The central lesson is to identify what is distorted before choosing a metric.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Different fairness criteria protect different interests and can conflict.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Readers learn to examine consequential dependencies without expecting one universal fairness score.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Two matched users can receive similar final answers after very different agent journeys.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: One may receive additional research, a tool call, or escalation to a human.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The other may receive none of those resources.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book treats those choices as allocations that ordinary text benchmarks can miss.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That example explains why its account extends from model behavior to complete workflows.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A predictive target can reflect an institution's assumptions rather than the outcome people actually need.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Medical spending can reflect access to care, instead of how much care someone needs.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: When access differs, using spending as the target can reproduce that inequality.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That is why the book asks whose need a chosen measure actually represents.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Institutions remain responsible for choosing those standards, even when a model predicts them accurately.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Start with the distinctions between statistical bias, harmful disparities, and normative disagreement.
